summary: LUNAR HORIZON is a browser-based 3D adventure that takes players from mission preparation to exploration of a chosen world and a return journey. Before launch, players select one of six destinations: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Titan, or Pluto. The game presents NASA and NSSDCA reference values for the selected destination and adapts its lighting, colors, atmosphere, and gravity-based movement. Players complete interactive preparation tasks, launch, avoid meteors, land, and work through seven objective-based puzzles. Each objective connects gameplay to a relevant planetary fact, such as surface temperature, pressure, sunlight, distance, day length, gravity, or escape velocity. NASA mission and launch-vehicle facts also appear during flight. The figures are embedded reference information, not a live NASA feed; planetary scenery and terrain are generated by the game and are not NASA maps.

PROJECT DETAILS

LUNAR HORIZON is an interactive 3D browser game about preparing for, carrying out, and returning from a fictional Moon mission. Players begin at home and drive through a city to a space center, following GPS directions and objective markers. At the center, they complete mission preparation tasks involving a medical check, spacesuit and helmet, oxygen system, communications, navigation, and launch controls. These tasks use short interactive puzzles, including connecting wires, routing pipes, tightening screws, operating switches, calibrating controls, and solving sequence challenges.

After launch, players steer around meteors while monitoring spacecraft damage, then control the landing engines. On the Moon, a minimap and visible markers guide players through seven outpost objectives: a solar array, greenhouse, radiation shelter, communications site, research area, sample collection, and planting a flag. Each objective is paired with a small puzzle. A timed solar-storm alert directs the player to the radiation shelter. After completing the lunar objectives, the player returns to Earth, lands by parachute, is welcomed by a crowd, and drives home to finish the story.

The game includes an in-game NASA reference panel. During the launch, flight, landing, lunar-surface, and return scenes, the panel displays NASA-published figures and mission information: SLS Block 1 height and thrust; Saturn V height and thrust; the average Earth–Moon distance; lunar gravity and escape velocity; lunar day and night temperature extremes; an Apollo parking-orbit and translunar-injection example; Artemis Base Camp concept elements; Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39B; and Orion’s lunar-return speed and heat-shield temperature. NASA source links are listed in the NASA Data section below. The panel uses fixed reference facts embedded in the game code, not a live API or spacecraft telemetry. The displayed remaining distance and altitude are simplified game estimates. The lunar terrain and structures are procedurally generated and are not mapped from NASA imagery or elevation data.

The project is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules, and Three.js 0.160.0, loaded from jsDelivr. It also uses Three.js add-ons, browser speech synthesis, and the Web Audio API. Visual textures, terrain, and sound effects are generated in code. The game offers an optional local audio-file input for the ending; any recording included in a published demo should be credited separately.
